canonicalTeaching.requirement: Identity links the source, product and intended recipient; the source and recipient are the same person in the illustrated fictional autologous case.

A timing comparison needs its start and end events: collection-to-infusion, order-to-infusion, enrolment-to-infusion, receipt-to-release and culture duration are different clocks. Use elapsed calendar days and state how repeat collections and the spread are handled. In a fictional workflow only, collection and culture begin on day 0, culture ends on day 7, release occurs on day 12 and infusion on day 18. The seven-day culture interval is inside an eighteen-day collection-to-infusion interval; it does not describe the whole pathway.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Autologous cells come from the intended recipient; allogeneic cells come from another person. This source distinction is separate from whether engineering occurs outside or inside the body and from whether a cell product or a carrier is administered. Donor-cell manufacture can provide inventory for later recipients, but usable supply, quality disposition, matching requirements, preparation and clinical eligibility still govern access. Ex vivo describes engineering outside the body followed by administration of a cell product. In vivo engineering administers an instruction-carrying product and generates modified cells inside the body; it is not the same as testing an ex vivo product in an animal. Location, recipient versus donor origin and transient versus stable genetic fate are separate attributes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Qasim's 2017 report described two infants given donor CAR T cells edited at TRAC and CD52, with lymphodepletion including an anti-CD52 antibody and subsequent allogeneic transplantation. Benjamin's 2020 report combined early cohorts of seven children and fourteen adults; graft-versus-host disease, cytokine release syndrome, infections and treatment-related deaths were reported. A source or edit label does not eliminate clinical risks. These are small, uncontrolled reports, and their participant counts must not be added to later overlapping CALM analyses.

The cited preclinical results do not by themselves establish a fixed cost reduction, universal absence of lymphodepletion or automatic repeat-dose feasibility. Evaluate the actual process, monitoring and protocol rather than treating these as inherent benefits of all in vivo products.
